title: SSID, WPA2/WPA3 authentication and guest networks

videos.script: Every wireless network announces itself by name. {{beacon}} Anyone in range can hear that name. Anyone in range can also hear the traffic that follows it, because on a wireless network the air is the cable. {{air}} So a wireless network has to answer two questions that a wired one mostly skips. Who is allowed on? And how do the people who are not allowed on fail to read what everybody else sends? {{questions}} This lesson follows the answers in the order they were built. First WPA2-Personal, where everybody shares one passphrase, and why a short one is a real risk. {{wpa2}} Then WPA3, which makes a recording of the air far less useful to anybody who steals one. {{wpa3}} Then the enterprise version. Each person signs in with their own account, gets their own key, and can be removed without changing anybody else's. {{enterprise}} Last, the network for visitors. A guest network is not a second password. It is a separate network, with its own VLAN and its own rules. {{guest}} This lab has no radio, so nothing in this lesson is captured. You will work from the standards, from numbers you can compute yourself, and from configuration you can read. {{config}}
